## Introduction

> “90% of my skills just went to zero dollars and 10% of skills just went up a 1000x.” What are those 10% skills? “Having a vision, to be able to set milestones towards that vision, keeping track of the design to maintain the levels of complexity or control the levels of complexity as you go forward.”

There’s no shortage of opinions right now on how software should be built. Like most of us on X, I’m watching from the sidelines, testing out new workflows and exploring the ideas posted. There are already great discussions happening about this, but there is always room to explore further how we build the underlying skills and core judgment, and then communicate it, and get better at it in a way that outlasts any workflow.

In short, the solution I am betting on is a shift toward mainstream, detailed case studies, much like the one I share below, so that judgment can be displayed, evaluated, and improved in public. Consultants have been doing this for a while, and many senior software engineering roles already rely on it during hiring. But the days of showing just two or three screenshots and a simple link to previous work and a short description have come to an end.

Showing the outcome of a product in these times may not be enough. People used to immediately realize how much effort and thought you put into a project when you showed them a final walkthrough. Now, you are left open to being second-guessed on whether the project was actually well thought out. The person viewing your product is tasked with understanding the domain and putting in the effort to see if you have sound judgment, something they are unlikely to do, because it is so hard to test a person's judgment from an isolated result. Judgment needs to compound and form a predictable pattern so that others can truly believe you can implement the same pattern in their projects. Ultimately, this means we need to share parts of our thinking process that we are not usually familiar with, which can certainly feel a bit vulnerable, but it gives us an opportunity to communicate our judgment, open a window to the public, and allow for valuable feedback to sharpen and improve it.

## Find the goal

### The business and customer journey

Our case study is for an HVAC company based in the United Kingdom. They have been operating for five years installing and servicing heating and cooling equipment on businesses, real estate, and private property. They communicate with customers mainly through email and keep their data in spreadsheets. As the business grows, keeping track of customers has become harder over the years.

The owner has considered using a standard CRM featuring an email pipeline that syncs conversations and automatically populates customer names. However, the client bets on the fact that more can be done if we are able to analyze data within the email before it reaches a CRM.

To go deeper into what the client plans to understand from their mailbox, we have to understand how the business operates. The enterprise functions as one large continuous loop, stretching from generating work and receiving payments to reinvesting revenue into generating more work.

Within this operational cycle, every job follows a specific path from start to finish. The flow diagram below outlines the complete progression of how an incoming opportunity turns into a completed job.

### The client’s bet

The client bets on re-engaging customers with expiring warranties to secure repeat servicing. Although individual service visits rarely turn a profit on their own, profitability becomes achievable when bundling multiple jobs in the same neighborhood or pairing them with a nearby installation, which cuts down on travel time and transportation expenses.

After getting all this background on the business and the client's bet, we need to set a goal that lets us constantly check if we are actually moving toward it. Establishing this goal brings structure and clarity, sitting right in the sweet spot of not being too broad or too narrow, which gives us the flexibility to switch bets if the current one doesn't pan out.

So below is the goal.

The business has five years of customers sitting unreachable in the Gmail mailboxes of several people. The goal is to get them out in a form the business can act on.

It clearly defines what we plan to do, not too narrow, but not too broad either.

### Elements, connectors and bottlenecks

Our goal functions as a distinct unit within a system. My notes in Systems Thinking give me a way to break this down into three key concepts:

- elements (actors). The partakers in the system.

- connectors. The relationships between those elements.

- bottlenecks within the connectors. The friction points that affect how those relationships actually function.

## Make it work

### Kickoff

Our order of work is borrowed from Sam Bhagwat’s Principles of Building AI Agents : make it work, make it right, make it fast, a philosophy widely attributed to Kent Beck.

- make it work. Get an email thread through the workflow and produce a record I can inspect.

- make it right. Check the analyzed records against its sources and the client’s expectations. Find the mistakes and revise the system.

- make it fast. Run more email threads through it and find which constraints appear under load and find ways it can scale to process more email threads.

- make it useful. Run continuous Product Discovery through interviews, and make bets based on what the underlying system is capable of handling.

The last part (Make it useful) is my addition to Kent Beck's structure. Product discovery happens throughout the project, but giving it its own section makes room to look for opportunities where the extracted data can produce value. Similar parallels exist: some put 'Make it Useful' at the top, some at the end, and some treat it as continuous.

For this part, we divide the process into six stages and go through them one by one.

Database design

Choosing SQLite to store our data naturally leads to the next question, how should we design our database model? Drawing from Michael J. Hernandez’s Database Design for Mere Mortals , the process starts with a clear mission statement and objective, which aligns with our core extraction goals.

- mission objectives. Focused on extracting specific business requirements, identifying equipment installations, service locations, quote and invoice histories, and warranty timelines, to allow repeat job bundling.

- legacy database and storage. Consists of email back-and-forth and spreadsheets. When inspecting these current systems, Hernandez cautions against copying spreadsheet layouts directly into table structures, since these layouts often combine multiple distinct subjects that should instead be separated into relational tables.

- business workflow. Mapped across five core stages, enquiries → site visits → quotes → invoices → completed jobs.

Database design is inherently iterative and refined continuously throughout the design phases, but our logical design phase is now complete after multiple feedback loops, ending up with the database diagram below.

- Prepare (done)

- Filter (current step)

In the filtering phase, we need to remove emails unrelated to our core goal. These filtering opportunities are apparent by simply reviewing the email archive.

The bigger question is the age-old debate of deterministic versus AI filters. While the modern consensus favors a hybrid approach, we still have to ask: where should we draw the line, and what parts of the task can AI actually take over from traditional deterministic filters?

Instead of letting that assumption bias our approach again, let's keep it front and center while we first evaluate what a purely deterministic check can achieve and how far it can take us. Specifically, deterministic checks can easily filter out labeled Gmail messages and routine transactional business emails.

The mailbox after the deterministic checks

- Deterministic checks Transactional, promotions and marketing emails 27.1% removed

- Left for extraction The remaining emails that are ready for extraction 72.9% kept

Rather than adding a separate AI filter to clean out the remaining noise, I chose to let the extraction agent absorb it, trusting that it would only surface records when actual job data was present. We are not optimizing to eliminate all noise entirely; the goal is simply to extract relevant details, not to achieve zero noise.

Fast-forwarding to the results, letting the email extraction agent handle the remaining data paid off. While the agent was busy extracting relevant details, it indirectly categorized 11% of the emails as unrelated noise.

The mailbox after extraction

- Indirectly marked by the email agent Emails the deterministic checks missed, but the email agent indirectly caught 11.1% flagged later

- Customer mail The remaining emails that are ready for extraction 61.8% kept

- Extract details (current step)

To gather enough context regarding the data we need to extract, we ask ourselves and the client, what specific fields does the business need to know about a past customer or job, and exactly where within the messages are they located?

Based on our findings, the required fields are buried across different parts of the thread, some reside in the email body, others are located within attachments, and a few must be inferred from the conversation.

To figure out how to approach this set of extractions, we first needed to determine what pattern to use, adapting to the reality that certain groups of extractions could be handled by deterministic logic while others required an agent. As Antonio Gulli’s Agentic Design Patterns highlights, we shouldn't treat these patterns as an either-or choice; instead, we approach them as modular blocks you build upon along the way. In our case, we ended up using all the patterns, starting from basic prompt chaining to parallelization, routing, and finally agent-directed execution.

Fundamentally, this aligns with Anthropic’s perspective on building effective agents , where a workflow is defined by paths set in code. We know the desired end result because the output and the broad sequence are known beforehand, while the model is left to handle the interpretation within each step.

- Prompt chaining · sequence (chosen)

- Parallelization · concurrency (chosen)

- Routing · selection (chosen)

- Agent-directed execution · bounded tasks (chosen)
